text: Lesson 1 settled that hardened needs to mean something checkable, not a personal judgment call. The industry-standard way to get that is the CIS Benchmarks -- a consensus-built, vendor-independent set of hardening recommendations, published by the Center for Internet Security, covering Windows Server, major Linux distributions, and dozens of other platforms.

Each benchmark splits into Level 1, basic hardening with minimal business impact, and Level 2, stricter defense-in-depth hardening that can affect compatibility. Hartwell is a utility running production billing and outage-reporting systems -- breaking something during a first security project would cost more credibility than it buys. Mara scopes to CIS Level 1 for both Windows Server and the Linux distributions in use. Level 2 is a reasonable future step, not a day-one move.

A full CIS Benchmark runs hundreds of settings, and most don't even apply to these four machines. Scoping means picking the subset that matters for HRU-FILE01 and HRU-APP01 on Windows -- account lockout policy, disabled unused services, rotated local admin passwords, and Domain-profile firewall rules -- and for hru-web01 and hru-db01 on Linux -- SSH hardening, fail2ban, automatic security updates, and ufw rules.

Just as important is what's left off, in writing: CIS Level 2 settings, every other server Hartwell runs beyond this representative handful, and antivirus, vulnerability scanning, and patch tooling rollouts -- all real, valuable work, but each its own project, not something folded in silently here.

A 200-item checklist covering every setting everywhere mostly wouldn't get implemented correctly under time pressure, and Dale would have no way to tell what actually mattered. A dozen specific, verified checks against four named servers, each with a command to prove it landed, is something he can actually sign off on.
With the checklist scoped, next lesson applies it for real -- hardening the two Windows servers, one verified step at a time.
